newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish bonds still popular, but outlook less sure.
newsitem.headline: Danish bonds still popular, but outlook less sure.

text.p: A survey shows that Danish bonds are still popular with foreign buyers, but traders warn prices could be close to peaking for the current economic cycle.
The latest survey by French banker Paribas shows an increase in the number of investors overweight with Danish bonds at the end of September 1996 compared with a June survey.
"This can partly be explained by the strong support from German investors, who are attracted by the yield pick-up with virtually no currency risk," it said.
Paribas gives Denmark a rating of 67 on its new allocation scale -- where 50 is neutral -- compared with 63 in the previous survey.

But a Reuter poll of 15 Danish and foreign analysts predicts a period of stability, with the spread between benchmark 10-year Danish and German bond yields seen virtually unchanged at around 80 basis points a year from now, after an initial period of widening.
The 10-year benchmark price has shown a steady upward trend over the past three months, rising from 103.99 at the end of June to 108.61 on Wednesday.
The yield differential has narrowed from 99 basis points to 77 basis points over the same time.

Those predicting stability say Denmark's strong economy and solid crown currency will counterbalance the negative effect of its refusal for the time being to join European Economic and Currency Union.
Although one of a handful of countries economically qualified to join the coming monetary union, Denmark is bound by a "no' vote delivered by its people in a 1993 referendum.
Finance Minister Mogens Lykketoft estimates that the voters' rejection has added about 50 basis points to the yield gap between German and Danish bonds.
Many analysts say that the bond market will continue to pay a price for rejection of EMU until the government declares that it will seek a new referendum.
"Danish bond prices will be relatively worse off until we get a clear political signal from the government," Thomas Thygesen, Chief Economist at the Copenhagen branch of Svenska Handelsbanken said.

Some analysts argue that as the 1999 launch date for EMU approaches, its final makeup and details of how it will operate may make it less attractive than originally thought and make the Danish refusal to join an advantage rather than a burden.

"A lot of the momentum in European markets presupposes that EMU will take effect on January 1, 1999 with a reasonably broad membership. Should that assumption be proved incorrect over the next two years the market dynamic will change accordingly," an economist said.
Several believe that Denmark has the best of both worlds.

Shadowing the mark, meeting EMU economic performance criteria and probably enjoying a special relationship with the Euro through a new Exchange Rate Mechanism, will give it some of the advantages of membership they say, while insulating it from market ire should union not go ahead as or when planned.
